Bhāskara
------------------------------------------
The Vedānta system of philosophy based mainly on the Brahmasūtras, which itself is a systematization of the doctrines of the major उपनिषद्स्, gained greater currency and respectability due to शङ्कर (A.
-820). Out of the several post-शङ्कर Vedāntins, who criticised his views, भास्कर was one. Since Rāmānuja (A.
-1137) in turn criticises the views of भास्कर, the latter may have lived prior to him, around A.

.
Bhāskara wrote a commentary on the Brahmasūtras, the Bhāskara-bhāṣya, wherein he has expressed his views. His school is generally called the Bhedā-bhedavāda, a doctrine that upholds the reality of both unity and multiplicity.
This world of souls and matter is a real evolution of ब्रह्मन्. ब्रह्मन् is not an undifferentiated mass of चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स्. In the causal state, it is a unity and in the evolved state it is a multiplicity. In its causal and generic aspect, this world is non-different from ब्रह्मन्, but different as effects and individuals. Both are equally real.
Matter as evolved into bodies and senses acts on ब्रह्मन् as an उपाधि or limiting adjunct and results in the rise of the jīvas or individual souls. However, the jīvas are related to ब्रह्मन् as sparks to fire and are atomic in size. The life of सṁसार or bondage brought about by transmigration is due to the confusing between ब्रह्मन् and the upādhis. Libe-ration comes through कर्म or actions prescribed by the वेदस्, done in the right spirit, and ज्ञान or knowledge of the सोउल् that arises in the मिन्द् purified by कर्म. Thus he advocates ज्ञान-कर्म-samuccaya or a balanced combination of action and knowledge.
There was another भास्कर, who probably lived in the 7th century A. D. He was the author of two works on astronomy—Mahābhāskarīya and Laghu-bhāskarīya—which were used for astronomical calculations in South India upto the end of the 15th century.

Bhāsa
------------------------------------------
Bhāsa is one of the reputed authors known to the writers of ancient classical literature in Sanskrit. Though mentioned by कालिदास and बाण, his works had not been traced. It was only in 1912 that Paṇḍit गणपति Śāstri of Trivandrum published 13 plays like Pratijña Yaugandarāyaṇa and Svapnavāsavadatta. After several rounds of controversies among the Sanskrit scholars, it is now generally agreed that all these 13 plays are by a single author and that it could be भास, though the evidence is not conclusive. He might have been a contemporary of पाणिनि, the grammarian, and might have lived in the 4th century B. C., but in a place far away from his.
Very little is known of his life. He was probably a ब्राह्मण-मुनि and had strong leanings towards the विष्णु cult.
Six of his plays like Madhyama Vyāyoga, Karṇabhāra and Ūrubhaṅga are based on the Mahābhārata and two (Pratimā and Abhiṣeka) on the रामायण.
The rest like Svapnavāsavadatta and Avimāraka are from miscellaneous sources like the Bṛhatkathā of Guṇāḍhya, an ancient collection of tales in the Paiśācī language.
Bhāsa’s language is simple, direct and forceful. The dramas are eminently suited to be enacted on the stage.

Bhāskara-rāya
------------------------------------------
Worship of God as मोथेर् is an ancient practice in India. Though the references to the मोथेर्-cult are very meagre in the early Vedic literature, we have plenty of material in the later पुराणस् and तन्त्रस्. One of the most famous texts of the मोथेर्-cult, which is very popular in South India is the Lalitāsahasranāma, which again is a part of the Brahmāṇḍapurāṇa. The most celebrated commentary on this text is the Saubhāgyabhāskara of भास्कर-राय-makhin (also known as Bhāsurānanda-nātha). He lived during the 17th-18th centuries. His spiritual preceptor was नरसिṁह Adhvarī who taught him 18 kinds of sciences. An adept in several fields like the Vedānta, Mīmāṁsā, व्याकरण (grammar) and mantraśāstra (science of mantras) he is said to have composed 42 works. The works Varivasyā-rahasya and Setubandha along with the Saubhāgya-bhāskara are considered as the ‘prasthānatraya’ or the three basic texts of Śrīvidyā, the मोथेर्-cult of South India.

Bhāṣāpariccheda
------------------------------------------
This is a well-known and popular treatise on the न्याय-Vaiśeṣika philo-sophy by Viśvanātha Nyāyapañcānana Bhaṭṭācārya (17th Century A. D.) who lived in नवद्वीप (in Bengal).
The author himself has written a detailed commentary, Siddhāntamuktāvalī by name.
There are 168 verses in the anuṣṭubh metre.
The work, which is quite a tough one, deals with the following topics: the seven categories (saptapadārthas); the substances (dravyas); the five methods of knowledge like प्रत्यक्ष or direct perception; मिन्द्; qualities (guṇas); some details about inference (anumāna); some miscellaneous qualities.

Bhāskarācārya
------------------------------------------
A celebrated astronomer and mathematician, भास्कराचार्य (A.

-1160) wrote the monumental work Siddhānta-śiromaṇi when he was only 36. It has four chapters of which the first—called Līlāvatī—is on arithmetic. The story goes that he named this part of his work after his daughter Līlāvatī who was widowed at an early age, to immortalize her. An extremely popular work written in an interesting and entertaining manner, it has been translated into several languages over the centuries. It includes sections on śūnya or ज़ेरो, geometry, mensuration, and kuṭṭaka or indeterminate equations of the first magnitude. Bījagaṇita or algebra is the second chapter. The other two chapters called Gaṇitādhyāya and Golādhyāya are works on अस्त्रोनोम्य् that include celestial mathematics.
The work has several commentaries in Sanskrit.
Another work of his, called Kāraṇa-kutūhala, a handbook for preparing astronomical tables, is not so well-known.

Bhasma-jābālopaniṣad
------------------------------------------
One of the minor उपनिषद्स् of the Atharvaṇaveda group, Bhasmajābālopa-niṣad is in the form of a long conversation between the sage Jābāla-Bhusuṇḍi and Lord शिव. It is in prose and consists of two chapters.
The sage Jābāla approaches Lord शिव with great reverence and inquires of him thus:
Please teach me all about भस्म (holy ash) including the mode of wearing the त्रिपुण्ड्र (religious mark of three lines drawn on the forehead) by which मोक्ष or लिबेरतिओन् can be easily obtained.
Kindly enlighten me about the daily duties of a ब्राह्मण in detail.
The reply given by the Lord शिव may be summarised as follows:
Before sunrise, fresh cowdung is to be collected on a palāśa leaf (Butea frondos), dried and then reduced to ashes in the gṛhya fire duly established, using materials like sesame or paddy soaked in ghee, which should be offered into the fire with appropriate mantras like tryambakaṁ yajāmahe and somāya स्वाहा. The ashes, after being consecrated through the गायत्री-मन्त्र, should be collected in a pot made of gold or silver or even mud. Taking some of it in the palm of the left hand, it should be applied on all parts of the body like the head, forehead, ears, neck, arms, chest and navel, repeating the mantras prescribed for each of the application.
In case the duly prepared भस्म is not available, the भस्म gathered from a च्रेमतिओन् ground or any other place may be used after purifying it with appropriate mantras.
Applying the भस्म as prescribed is a sacred and compulsory duty for a ब्राह्मण. If he fails to do so he incurs sin which has to be expiated by the repetition of the गायत्री-मन्त्र, while standing in water and ड़स्तिन्ग्. However, if he does it as prescribed, he will be freed from all sins, and obtains the fruits of पिल्ग्रिमगे to all the holy places as also a long life.
As for the daily duties of a ब्राह्मण the Lord शिव gives a detailed procedure for bath, putting on clean washed clothes, anointing with भस्म and wearing रुद्राक्ष beads.
This is then followed by instructions for worshipping the शिवलिङ्ग (the emblem of शिव). This has to be done thrice a day. meditation on Lord शिव’s form, bathing the लिङ्ग with water as also the भस्म and worship with the बिल्व (Aegle marmelos) leaves, are its constituents.
Next, the Lord teaches the मन्त्र of six letters (Oṁ namaś śivāya) and the मन्त्र of eight letters (Oṁ namo mahā-devāya). These are called ‘tārakamantras’ since they help the human being to cross (tāraka = that which helps one to cross) the ocean of सṁसार or transmigration.
Then comes a description of शिव as ब्रह्मन्, followed by the assertion that knowledge of शिव-रुद्र leads to मोक्ष or लिबेरतिओन्.
Lord शिव is the support of the whole च्रेअतिओन्. He is the one who liberates the living beings from bondage. Those who are unable to realize this, should go to काशी and live there till death. Such votaries of शिव who live in काशी should never swerve from the path of truth and never miss smearing भस्म on their bodies, wearing रुद्राक्ष beads and worshipping Him through the लिङ्ग, which is ‘jyotirliṅga’ or ‘liṅga of light’. Such worship and meditation on him will confer results like freedom from sins, sorrows and sufferings. He will ultimately attain मुक्ति or लिबेरतिओन्. Failure to worship Lord शिव at काशी thus, will entail sin which has to be expiated through bath, ड़स्तिन्ग् and chanting of the Rudra (a section from the Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda).
Lord शिव utters the तारकमन्त्र (Oṁ namaśśivāya) into the ears of those dying at काशी, thus liberating them from सṁसार or transmigration.
The upaniṣad concludes with a warning to those that live at काशी, but transgress the prescribed mode of living. But they too will be liberated after suffering and repentance.
See also UPANIṢADS.

bhasma
(‘that which shines,’ ‘that which destroys all sins,’ ‘that which produces auspiciousness,’ ‘ashes’)
------------------------------------------
Fire is believed to reduce all substances to their primal state of purity. Hence, भस्म or ashes have always been considered as sacred by certain sections of the Hindu society, especially the Śaivas and the Śāktas (followers of शिव and शक्ति or the Divine मोथेर्).
Bhasma derived from the Vedic fires is called ‘Śrauta-भस्म.’ It is to be taken out of the fire when the Vedic ritual is in progress and applied on the body. That derived from the fire lit up during a ritual performed as per the directions of smṛtis (secondary scriptures like the धर्म-śāstras) is called ‘smārta-भस्म.’ If the fire is kindled by the अघोर-मन्त्र (a मन्त्र describing the अघोर or non-fierce aspect of शिव) with the wood of the बिल्व tree (Aegle marmelos), the ashes are called ‘śivāgni-भस्म.’ This भस्म is considered to be extremely sacred and capable of destroying sins as also ritual impurities.
Wearing a ‘tripuṇḍra,’ a mark of three lines on the forehead with भस्म, using the fingers on the right hand (the thumb, the middle finger and the ring finger) is considered a must for all the devotees of शिव. These three lines are supposed to represent: the three वेदस् (Ṛg, Yajus and Sāman); the three syllables (a, u and ma) of Om; the three guṇas (sattva, रजस् and तमस्); the three śaktis or powers (kriyāśakti, इच्छाशक्ति and ज्ञानशक्ति) of देवी or Divine मोथेर्; the three pressings of सोम juice in सोमयाग (prātassavana, mādhyandinasavana and tṛtīyasavana) and so on. The whole idea seems to be to bring into one’s मिन्द्, various religio-spiritual concepts so as to feel pure and elevated.
Bhasma may be smeared over other parts of the body also, often to the accompaniment of appropriate mantras, thus purifying both the body and the मिन्द्. This is sometimes called भस्म-स्नान or bath with भस्म.
Among the liṅgāyats (śaivites of Karnataka State) भस्म-dhāraṇa or applying the त्रिपुण्ड्र of भस्म on the forehead is considered as an important act of practice classed under ‘aṣṭāvaraṇas.’ (See AṢṬĀVARAṆAS.) According to their philosophy, भस्म is really that which burns up all illusions and paves the way for the intuition of the inner Self. The ashes are only an external and gross symbol of the process.
Bhasma as consecrated ash is used for ritual purification (like the water of the गङ्गा river) of objects defiled by the touch of undesirable (or sinful) persons or animals etc., for protection against inauspicious things or evil spirits or even for purposes of sorcery and magical rites.
Bhasma has to be prepared by burning cowdung cakes in fire with appropriate mantras. The process has been described in the Bhasma-jābalopaniṣad, one of the minor उपनिषद्स् of the Śaiva cult.
